items.prompt: Explain one possible consumer benefit of competitive pressure where sellers offer close alternatives.
items.canonical_answer: A firm may limit its price or improve value to retain buyers (1), because consumers can switch to rival offers if its terms are unattractive (1).
marking_guidance: Benefit for household: better value/price pressure, 1; because: switching to rivals disciplines seller, 1.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation on a monopolist’s ability to raise price while maintaining sales.
items.canonical_answer: Higher price may reduce the quantity buyers are willing and able to purchase (1), because the firm remains constrained by demand despite having no direct rival (1).
marking_guidance: Limitation for firm: quantity loss, 1; because: demand constrains price-output combination, 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Evaluate whether customers necessarily benefit when a sole supplier expands output enough to lower unit costs but has discretion over its price.
items.canonical_answer: Argument for: larger output may spread costs and support investment, making lower prices or improved service feasible. Argument against: weak rivalry may let the firm retain savings as higher profit, while demand constrains customers’ choices. Judgement: customers benefit if realised savings translate into affordable prices or better service; lower unit cost alone does not prove that condition is met.
marking_guidance: Argument for: scale/investment mechanism up to 3; argument against: weak rivalry/pass-through limitation up to 3; judgement with condition on actual consumer gain up to 2 = 8.

items.prompt: Define perfect competition at the simple model level.
items.canonical_answer: A market model with many small buyers and sellers of identical products, relevant information and free entry/exit, where individual firms take the market price.
marking_guidance: Definition: many sellers/identical product, 1; distinguishing qualifier: assumptions supporting individual price taking, 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Define monopoly at the simple model level.
items.canonical_answer: A market with a single supplier and barriers preventing effective entry into that market.
marking_guidance: Meaning: single supplier, 1; qualifier: relevant market and entry barriers, 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: In a market, many small sellers offer identical standard containers. Buyers know the available prices and can change seller easily. A separate island repair market has one supplier because establishing the required workshop is costly. Its buyers can reduce use when prices rise. (a) Describe three relevant market features (6). (b) Examine how pricing discretion differs (7). (c) Suggest what evidence is needed before deciding which arrangement benefits customers more (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Many container sellers provide alternatives. Identical products and price information support switching. The repair market has a sole supplier protected by costly entry, but demand is still responsive. (b) A container seller cannot assume buyers pay more for an identical product when informed alternatives exist; it takes the market price under the stated model. The repairer has greater discretion, yet a higher price can reduce use. Entry barriers do not remove the demand constraint. Neither model guarantees low production costs. (c) Compare actual prices, service quality, access and costs. Investigate whether sole-supplier scale savings exist and reach customers, and whether the container market’s assumptions apply in practice. The judgement should use consumer outcomes rather than seller count alone. A sole supplier could provide valuable efficient service, while weak rivalry could also permit poor value.
marking_guidance: Context: containers/repair. Parts/allocation: (a) three developed features 2 each = 6. (b) price-taking mechanism 3, monopoly discretion/demand constraint 3, cost boundary 1 = 7. (c) outcome evidence 3, savings/pass-through 2, conditional judgement 2 = 7.

items.prompt: (a) Define a price taker (2). (b) Define monopoly (2). (c) Explain why identical products matter in perfect competition (2). (d) Explain why information matters to switching (2). (e) Explain why an individual competitive firm still chooses output (2). (f) Explain why monopoly does not mean unlimited sales at any price (2). (g) Explain one possible gain from sole-supplier scale (2). (h) Explain why a cost saving does not prove consumer benefit (2).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Firm accepting the market price because its individual influence is negligible. (b) Single supplier protected by entry barriers in the defined market. (c) Buyers can obtain the same product elsewhere, limiting an individual markup. (d) Knowledge of alternatives lets buyers compare and act on offers. (e) The firm must decide how much to produce given price, resources and costs. (f) Buyers’ willingness and ability constrain quantity at the chosen price. (g) Large output may spread costs or fund equipment, improving productive possibilities. (h) Savings may be retained rather than passed on through price or quality.
marking_guidance: Parts/allocation and precision: eight at 2 each. (a) market price + negligible influence; (b) single seller + entry barrier; (c) same product + switching discipline; (d) knowledge + comparison; (e) output decision + constraints; (f) demand + price-quantity limit; (g) scale mechanism + possible gain; (h) lower costs + uncertain pass-through.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: The Bay Equipment Hire firm is the sole supplier in a defined remote market because duplicating its specialised equipment is costly. It proposes a higher hire price to finance better maintenance. Some customers can postpone hiring. No cost figures or service-improvement evidence is supplied. (a) Define monopoly (2). (b) Explain two limits on the firm’s price-output choice (4). (c) Explain how weak competition could affect customers (7). (d) Discuss whether the higher price is justified by the stated proposal (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) A single supplier with barriers preventing effective entry in its market. (b) Higher price can reduce hire quantity as customers postpone. Costs constrain whether the chosen price and output generate sufficient receipts relative to resources used. (c) With no direct rival, switching pressure is reduced and the firm may have less incentive to keep prices low or respond to complaints. Entry barriers can sustain that position. However, specialised equipment and large scale may provide service that would be costly to duplicate. Customers benefit only if productive possibilities improve actual access, price or quality. (d) Funding maintenance could improve reliability and reduce interruption for customers. Against it, the proposal lacks cost or improvement evidence, and reduced rivalry may allow a rise without a matching gain. A supported decision requires evidence of the maintenance need, credible improvements and affordability effects. The proposal alone is insufficient to establish justification; accept a stronger case if verified service gains warrant the burden.
marking_guidance: Context: Bay Equipment. Parts/allocation: (a) single supplier 1, market/entry qualifier 1. (b) demand and cost constraints, each mechanism + implication 2 = 4. (c) weak-rivalry mechanism 3, possible productive gain 2, consumer pass-through boundary 2 = 7. (d) service case 2, evidence/access limitation 2, conditional judgement 3 = 7.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a town should judge a market with many sellers better for customers than a sole supplier solely from the number of firms (9).
items.canonical_answer: For: many alternatives can strengthen switching pressure, discouraging unattractive prices and poor service. Under the perfect-competition assumptions, individual sellers take the market price. Against: seller count does not establish identical products, good information or low costs. A sole supplier may gain from scale or specialised investment, though weak rivalry may allow savings to be retained. Judgement: compare actual affordability, quality, access and efficiency under the relevant conditions. The condition for a competition-based consumer benefit is effective rivalry and usable alternatives, while a scale-based defence requires realised gains reaching customers. Numbers alone do not resolve those questions.
marking_guidance: Argument for: switching/price discipline developed, up to 4. Argument against: missing assumptions and possible scale gains with limits, up to 4. Judgement: distinct condition based on actual consumer outcomes, 1. Total 9.
